subject: Cloud Computing
title: When to Choose IaaS
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on When to Choose IaaS.

hook.text: Your team needs custom OS configurations, specific kernel modules, and full root access. IaaS is the answer.

buildup.text: IaaS is best when you need maximum control over every layer of the stack.

discovery.text: Legacy app migrations often land on IaaS — the apps expect a traditional server environment.

twist.text: IaaS requires a team that can manage servers, security, and scaling. Without that, it's dangerous.

climax.text: If you have the ops team and need the control, IaaS gives you exactly what on-prem did — minus the hardware.

punchline.text: Choose IaaS when you need control and have the team for it.

quiz.question: When is IaaS the best cloud model choice?
options: When you need full control over OS, networking, and configuration
When you want the simplest possible deployment with no management
When you only need a ready-to-use application like email

details.summary: Choose IaaS when you need full control over the operating system, custom networking, or must run legacy applications that cannot be containerized or modernized. It suits workloads with specific kernel requirements, compliance mandates, or complex multi-tier architectures.
details.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong service model wastes money and engineering effort. Knowing when IaaS is the right fit prevents both over-engineering and under-provisioning.
takeaways: Best for workloads requiring full OS-level control
Suits legacy apps that cannot be easily modernized
Ideal when compliance requires specific configurations

faq.question: When should you avoid IaaS?
faq.answer: Avoid IaaS for greenfield applications that could run on PaaS or serverless with less operational burden. If you do not need kernel-level access or custom OS packages, PaaS or containers reduce management overhead significantly.

faq.question: Is IaaS cheaper than on-premises?
faq.answer: For variable workloads, IaaS is typically cheaper because you pay only for what you use. For steady-state, high-utilization workloads, on-premises can be cheaper over multi-year periods. The total cost depends on utilization, staffing, and facility expenses.
